rv.q: They’re well versed in the language of social justice yet maintain enough distance to poke fun at it — “Purim-slash-them” — without losing their moral clarity.
In Can I Be Frank? the echoes between Maya and Bassichis are sometimes elusive, sometimes deafening, sometimes extremely funny, and always piercingly true.
At times, it’s hard to tell where Maya ends and Bassichis begins.
Based on the talent and sheer force of will informing this show, I wouldn’t rule out the possibility of Morgan Bassichis seeing that last wish come true.
Bassichis is going places, and Can I Be Frank? packs plenty of laughs into its ninety-minute running time as well as a powerful argument about the necessity of comedy in terrible times.

Bassichis ultimately finds their way into Maya's mindset with the guidance of director Sam Pinkleton, who established with Cole Escola's Oh, Mary! the ability to sculpt cohesion out of a wildly imaginative sense of humor.

Morgan Bassichis is a talented performer, wrapping the long microphone cord around their body like a loose scarf, but they shift uneasily between tribute act and a meta framework, stopping and starting the show repeatedly to provide context for newcomers and to share personal details from their own life
The amount of time wasted apologizing to the audience for the show was egregious.

vr.q: Can I Be Frank? is a masterclass in blending comedy, commentary, and history.
